output.name: Halun
output.gloss: the Kite for the Drowned Child

output.myth: When a child goes into the sea, the mother climbs to the cliff on the first still day, when the wind has finally let go of the water. She ties a small kite of sailcloth, no bigger than a gull's wing, and writes the child's name in the bridle knots. Hesk counts the string and lets out a little more, because a mother may ask that much. The kite climbs the way the drowned climb, slow and wet and looking back. But Tavo came off the north water laughing, and he took the line in his fist and pulled. The kite went on past the Leeward lamps and the trade boats, and it lodged in the Unflown, where the sailors say things lost go. Sil sees it some nights, a small square in the dark. Aun, who cut the first string, has never had the nerve to climb up and look. The mothers say the child is still holding on.
output.verse:
A child's kite goes up
past the last of the gulls' calls,
she still holds the line.
